column6: The commentary connects loss, a rightful share, and final reckoning; Daniel says Belshazzar was weighed in balances and found deficient, combining judgment with the market image.
The commentary identifies the saved by belief together with deeds; Jesus distinguishes saying “Lord” from doing the Father's will.
The commentary pairs belief with righteous action; James warns hearers to become doers of the word rather than deceive themselves by hearing alone.
The commentary makes sabr a shared practice; Paul names patience and bearing with one another in love as the conduct that preserves unity.
The commentary makes mutual advice a way of holding a community together; Jesus instructs a person to confront a sinning brother privately, and says listening can regain the brother.
The commentary joins correction with patience and self-restraint; Paul says to restore a person caught in transgression gently while watching oneself against temptation.
The commentary puts truth before sabr because speaking truth may carry a cost; Timothy is told to reprove, rebuke, and exhort with complete patience and teaching.
The commentary makes haqq the content of mutual counsel; Paul says love does not rejoice in wrongdoing but rejoices with truth.
The commentary describes sabr as holding fast for another; Paul says love bears, hopes, and endures all things.
The commentary's traits include work and patience; Revelation praises a church for its works, labor, and patient endurance while testing false claims.
The commentary pairs belief with righteous action; Peter urges believers to supplement faith with virtue and knowledge.
The commentary describes sabr as holding oneself steady; Peter's sequence joins self-control to steadfastness and steadfastness to godliness.
The commentary's virtues culminate in reciprocal counsel; Peter ends his sequence with brotherly affection and love.
The commentary calls patience a bitter medicine that forms the person; James says the testing of faith produces steadfastness.
The commentary treats sabr as remaining firm until its work is done; James says steadfastness should have its full effect, making the person complete.
The commentary says patient good can turn enmity into intimacy; Esau runs to embrace Jacob after their long estrangement and fear.
The commentary hears belief as security and counsel as something passed on; Jehoshaphat tells Judah to trust God and the prophets, with the promise that they will stand and prosper.

column5: a time to speak and be silent
column6: The commentary joins truthful counsel to self-restraint; Qohelet's paired times for silence and speech give a concrete limit and occasion for words.
The commentary ties work to limited time and the day of reckoning; Qohelet urges wholehearted work now, saying there is no work or knowledge in Sheol.

column5: a soft answer turns away anger
column6: The commentary imagines truthful counsel replacing dispute; Proverbs says a gentle answer turns away wrath, showing how speech can interrupt conflict.
The commentary says good conduct can turn an enemy into a friend; Proverbs instructs the reader to feed an enemy who is hungry.

The commentary reads kindness toward an enemy as reconciliation; Proverbs adds that feeding the enemy heaps coals on his head, a consequence often read as shame or repentance but whose force is debated.
The commentary links trust to safety on a journey; Moses recalls that God accompanied Israel through forty years of wilderness travel and they lacked nothing.
The commentary makes counsel reciprocal; Avot says that when two sit with words of Torah between them, the divine presence is among them.

column5: one good deed leads to another
column6: The commentary pictures good action as work that keeps its value and continues; Avot says one commandment brings another and the reward of a commandment is another commandment.

The commentary replaces a wage formula with mutual responsibility; the Talmud lists acts of kindness and making peace between people among deeds whose fruit is enjoyed now while their principal remains for the world to come.
The commentary joins faith to patience under hardship; Sirach tells the one serving God to trust in the Lord, hope in him, and expect his help.
The commentary joins belief with haqq and sabr; Wisdom says those who trust God will understand truth and the faithful will abide with him in love.
The commentary treats patience as staying on a road through hardship; Hebrews urges believers to run the race set before them with endurance.
The commentary makes truthful counsel a communal duty carried with sabr; Peter says to answer anyone asking about hope with gentleness and respect, keeping a good conscience.

column5: bear with and forgive one another
column6: The commentary's patience means holding together when people strain one another; Paul tells the community to bear with and forgive one another.
The commentary defines the exception by a completed pattern of belief, action, and patience; Jesus says the one who endures to the end will be saved.
The commentary says truth may bring hardship that requires sabr; Paul praises the community's steadfastness and faith amid persecutions and afflictions.

column5: Aramaic חסר; table sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary's khusr concerns loss and deficiency; Daniel's Aramaic says the king was weighed and found lacking, a close contextual echo whose root correspondence the table leaves unverified.
The commentary uses khusr for loss; Deuteronomy says Israel lacked nothing on its wilderness journey, a specific opposite use of the root candidate listed by the table.
The commentary hears iman as trust and security; this verse repeats the Hebrew root in “trust the Lord” and “be established,” a wordplay relevant to the ayah but not proof of cognacy.
The commentary labels righteous deeds with ṣ-l-ḥ; Jehoshaphat's line ends with the Hebrew verb for prospering, a possible sound correspondence whose biblical sense is success.
